If rural areas are arid and lack vegetation, the evapotranspiration deficit would be small and unable to explain the UHI.

A desert city (e.g., Phoenix) and its arid surroundings both have negligible evapotranspiration, so by the target's own premise the deficit 'would be small and unable to explain the UHI,' yet such cities still exhibit a pronounced nocturnal UHI—directly falsifying evaporative-cooling deficit as the

The problem asks for the SINGLE mechanism that best explains why the night-time UHI gap is larger in some cities than in others. SRC_001's stated single cross-city modulator is vegetation/irrigation/aridity (the evaporative contrast), but its own derivation shows aridity cuts the wrong way: it says

SRC_001's cross-city modulator (evaporative contrast via vegetation/aridity) is internally inconsistent with observed arid-city UHI: it asserts drier surroundings reduce the urban-rural evaporative contrast and thus weaken the nocturnal gap, but arid cities like Phoenix exhibit large nocturnal UHI.

Urban heating studies (e.g., Oke 1982; Sailor 2011) find anthropogenic heat emissions and high thermal-admittance building materials substantially raise nocturnal urban temperatures, so cross-city differences in energy use and material heat capacity—not primarily sky-view factor—can dominate the UHI
